title: Into the pit (Genesis 37:12–36)
hook: the brothers sell Joseph for twenty pieces of silver

segments.voice: Yesterday, the coat and the dreams: a favorite son and brothers who couldn't say hello. Your line was the coat caused trouble. Who did you give your attention to? Today, the trouble comes due. Day three hundred sixty-one.

Jacob sends Joseph on an errand: go and see if your brothers are well, out with the flocks, and bring me word. It's a long walk, days from home. Joseph gets lost in the fields, and a stranger has to point him the right way. Picture him on the last ridge, the boy in the coat, visible from a long way off. His brothers see him coming before he can see their faces. And one of them says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the dreamer cometh." By the time he reaches them, they've already decided what to do.
screen: `GO AND SEE IF YOUR BROTHERS ARE WELL.` → `THE COAT, SEEN FROM FAR OFF.` → `BEHOLD THE DREAMER COMETH.`

segments.voice: First, the plot. Come, the brothers say, let's kill him, throw him into a pit, say a wild beast ate him, and we'll see what becomes of his dreams. Reuben, the eldest, pushes back: don't kill him, just throw him in the pit. Genesis tells us why: he planned to come back later and rescue him. Second, the pit. They strip off the coat, that coat, and throw him into an old cistern. It's empty, the text says. No water in it. And then, in one of the coldest lines in Genesis, they sit down to eat bread. Third, the sale. A caravan comes by, carrying spices down to Egypt. Judah speaks up: what profit is there in killing our brother? Let's sell him; after all, he's our brother, our own flesh. And they pull him out of the pit and, in the Douay-Rheims, "sold him to the Ismaelites, for twenty pieces of silver." Then Reuben comes back to the pit, finds it empty, and tears his clothes. Fourth, the lie. The brothers kill a young goat, dip the coat in its blood, and send it to their father. Do you know this coat? Jacob, who once wore goatskins to deceive his own blind father, is now deceived by goat's blood on his son's coat. He tears his garments and refuses to be comforted. I will go down to my son mourning, he says. Christians have long read Joseph as a figure of Christ: the beloved son, sent by his father to his brothers, rejected by his own, and sold for silver. Sold by his own, and carried down into Egypt.
screen: `LET'S KILL HIM, AND SEE HIS DREAMS.` · `AN EMPTY PIT, NO WATER.` · `TWENTY PIECES OF SILVER.` · `GOAT'S BLOOD ON THE COAT.` · then, large: `SOLD BY HIS OWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for anyone trafficked or sold, or, if you don't pray, hold them in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Joseph's story is ancient, but it isn't over. Somewhere today, people are bought and sold, forced to work, kept from home, sometimes by people who should have protected them. You may never know their names. Picture one person far from home who can't leave. Stay with them through the bell. If you pray, you can ask for their freedom, and for someone to find them. The bell holds the time.
Into the pit. Joseph, stripped of his coat, thrown into an empty cistern by his brothers, and sold for twenty pieces of silver into Egypt.
Your line: sold by his own. Today, learn one thing about modern trafficking, or about a group working against it, so the story doesn't stay ancient. Day three hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: The Church keeps February 8, the feast of Saint Josephine Bakhita, a Sudanese woman sold into slavery as a child who became a Canossian sister, as a world day of prayer against human trafficking.

original.note: Hebrew: pit, cistern, a hole cut to hold rainwater. Joseph's was empty.

trapdoor: what you thought: jealous brothers play a cruel prank.
what it means: a beloved son, sent to check on his brothers, is stripped, thrown into a pit and sold by his own.
what a scholar hears: bor, an empty cistern; the goat's blood echoes Jacob's goatskins; Christians read Joseph as a figure of Christ sold for silver.

notes: Douay-Rheims Genesis 37:19 and the 37:28 phrase quoted from memory; confirm wording ('Ismaelites').
37:28 mentions both Madianite merchants and Ismaelites; the script simplifies to 'a caravan' and the quoted phrase. Confirm.
Paraphrases: 37:20 plot, 37:26–27 Judah ('what profit... he is our brother and our flesh'), 37:35 Jacob's mourning. Kept without quotation marks.
Joseph as a type of Christ (beloved son, sent to his brothers, sold for silver): a common patristic reading (e.g. Ambrose, On Joseph). Confirm attribution as 'Christians have long read'.
howItsDone: February 8, Saint Josephine Bakhita; International Day of Prayer and Awareness against Human Trafficking since 2015. Confirm. CCC 2414 (enslaving human beings forbidden).
